steps.title: Covalent bond
steps.body: A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms. Each atom contributes one electron to the shared pair. Both atoms achieve a full outer shell.

steps.title: Simple molecular substance
steps.body: A substance made up of separate molecules, each containing a fixed number of atoms joined by covalent bonds (e.g. H₂O, CO₂).

steps.title: Giant covalent structure
steps.body: A huge network of atoms all joined by covalent bonds in a giant lattice (e.g. diamond, graphite).

steps.title: Intermolecular forces
steps.body: Weak forces of attraction between molecules (NOT between atoms within a molecule). These are much weaker than covalent bonds.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A few covalent substances form giant covalent structures (macromolecules) where every atom is bonded to neighbouring atoms by strong covalent bonds in a huge network. Diamond Diamond: Each carbon atom forms 4 covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a rigid tetrahedral structure. This makes diamond very hard and gives it a very high melting point. Very hard - each atom bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3D structure Very high melting point (about 3550°C) - strong covalent bonds throughout Does NOT conduct electricity - no delocalised electrons (all electrons are used in bonding) Graphite Graphite: Each carbon atom forms 3 covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in layers. One electron per atom is delocalised. The layers can slide over each other. Soft and slippery - layers can slide because only weak intermolecular forces hold the layers together Used as a lubricant - layers slide easily Very high melting point - strong covalent bonds within each layer Conducts electricity - delocalised ele

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: The most common mistake: saying "covalent bonds are weak" when explaining low melting points. It is the intermolecular forces that are weak, NOT the covalent bonds Always specify "intermolecular forces between molecules" when explaining properties of simple molecular substances For diamond vs graphite questions, always mention the number of bonds per carbon atom AND delocalised electrons Graphite conducts because of delocalised electrons - do NOT say "free electrons" as this is less precise Graphene is a single layer of graphite - remember this for the exam When drawing dot and cross diagrams, make sure shared pairs are clearly shown in the overlap between atoms
